strengths: Clear motivation grounded in an interpretable analysis (logit-lens style projection of vision tokens), including a nice diagnostic showing that hallucinations often occur when top-1 predictions diverge from visually grounded candidates in the top-K.

The proposed method (ReVisiT) is simple, training-free, and requires no external models or extra forward passes, addressing a genuine practical limitation of prior intra-alignment baselines (VCD, M3ID, SID, DoLa) that incur up to ~2x inference overhead.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation across three hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, AMBER) and two modern LVLM backbones (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL), plus a generalization check to a Mixture-of-Experts model (DeepSeek-VL2), plus qualitative examples and an explicit inference-time comparison.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the effect of vocabulary-subset constraint, layer-selection strategy, and threshold α, which helps validate design choices and explains why naive full-vocabulary vision-token projection fails.
Good positioning relative to related work (pre-/post-/intra-alignment taxonomy) and honest discussion of limitations (over-reliance on visual cues, no external knowledge correction).
weaknesses: Reported gains over the strongest baselines are often small and inconsistent across metrics/settings (e.g., CHAIRS on Qwen2.5-VL 31.6 vs Greedy 32.2 is a marginal difference; ReVisiT is not best on Recall, Cover, or several individual POPE/AMBER sub-metrics), making it hard to assess whether improvements are robust rather than within noise.

No variance/significance reporting for the main benchmark results (single greedy decoding run per method per dataset); only the latency experiment reports standard deviations, leaving open whether reported differences are statistically meaningful.

Key hyperparameters (layer pool: 'last' vs 'all'; threshold α) are selected per-model and per-task via what appears to be manual tuning without a principled selection procedure or held-out validation protocol described in the main text, raising concerns about generalizability to unseen models/tasks and about fair comparison (baselines use their published defaults, while ReVisiT’s hyperparameters seem more extensively tuned).

The theoretical grounding for why projecting intermediate vision-token hidden states through the LM head yields meaningful, vocabulary-constrained semantic signals is largely empirical/qualitative (a few case studies); no deeper analysis of failure modes or when this projection breaks down beyond the single ablation showing catastrophic failure without vocabulary constraint.

Method is a fairly direct combination of existing ingredients (DoLa-style early-exit contrastive logits, adaptive top-p style vocabulary constraint from Li et al. 2023, and JSD-based reference selection) applied to vision tokens instead of intermediate LLM layers, which somewhat limits conceptual novelty relative to the empirical contribution.

Evaluation of generalization is limited to one additional MoE model with only CHAIR metric and a repetition-penalty adjustment applied to all methods, which is a relatively narrow additional generalization check.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated: reusing vision-token hidden states (already computed) as internal reference signals via logit-lens projection avoids the extra forward passes required by VCD/M3ID/SID/DoLa, giving a genuine efficiency advantage (1-3% overhead vs. up to 2x for baselines, backed by repeated-run latency measurements with std. dev.).

Evaluation spans three established hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, AMBER) and two distinct LVLM backbones (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL), plus an additional MoE model (DeepSeekVL2), showing an attempt at broad generality.

The paper includes a reasonably transparent method description with pseudocode (Algorithm 1), an ablation study, and appendix material with exact numerical logit values supporting the qualitative claims in Figures 1-2.
The problem (visually ungrounded generation in LVLMs) is relevant to the NLP/multimodal community and the method is training-free and model-agnostic, which is a practically appealing property.
weaknesses: The ablation study (Table 4) reveals that most of the behavior change comes from the adaptive vocabulary-subset constraint itself (borrowed essentially from contrastive decoding [38]) — without it, generation catastrophically collapses. Crucially, there is no control ablation isolating vanilla greedy decoding restricted to the same constrained subset (without vision-token re-weighting) to demonstrate the marginal contribution of the vision-token selection mechanism versus the vocabulary truncation trick alone. This leaves the core contribution's actual causal effect ambiguous.

Reported improvements are frequently marginal and inconsistent across benchmarks/metrics: e.g., POPE accuracy for Qwen2.5-VL barely moves (84.49 -> 84.77), AMBER shows M3ID and SID beating ReVisiT on several sub-metrics (Cover, Cog, Hal) for LLaVA-1.5, and CHAIRS on LLaVA-1.5 ties exactly with SID (50.6). The claim of 'competitive or superior' results is not strongly substantiated by consistent wins.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting is provided for the main hallucination-benchmark results (only inference-speed measurements are averaged over repeated runs), making it hard to assess whether the reported gains are reliable rather than noise, especially given how small many deltas are.

The comparison may not be entirely fair: baselines use 'default hyperparameters from their original implementations,' while ReVisiT's vocabulary threshold α is explicitly tuned per task/benchmark. This asymmetry in hyperparameter search effort could inflate ReVisiT's apparent advantage.

Missing comparisons to several more recent/stronger intra-alignment or attention-based hallucination-mitigation baselines mentioned in the related work (e.g., OPERA, HALC, attention-calibration methods), limiting the strength of the 'state-of-the-art' comparison claim.

Qualitative analysis (Figures 4, 6) relies on a small number of cherry-picked examples rather than systematic human evaluation, which is insufficient to support claims about improved semantic/contextual understanding.

The method still requires computing JSD across all vision tokens and candidate layers at every decoding step; while claimed to avoid 'additional forward passes,' the actual computational complexity of this selection process (especially for models with many vision tokens, e.g., 576 for LLaVA) is not clearly characterized beyond empirical latency numbers, leaving reproducibility of the efficiency claims across different token counts/resolutions uncertain.

strengths: Novel and elegant core idea: instead of requiring additional forward passes (as in VCD, M3ID, SID) or auxiliary models, ReVisiT reuses the hidden states of vision tokens already computed during the single forward pass, projecting them via 'logit lens' into a dynamically constrained vocabulary and selecting the most relevant one via JSD to refine the output distribution. This yields a practically appealing training-free, near-zero-overhead decoding method.

Strong and well-documented efficiency results: measured per-token latency shows only 1-3% overhead versus vanilla greedy decoding, compared to ~2x overhead for DoLa/VCD/M3ID/SID, directly supporting the paper's central efficiency claim (Figure 3, Table 7).

Reasonably comprehensive empirical validation: three hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, AMBER) across two different LVLM backbones (LLaVA-1.5 and Qwen2.5-VL), plus an additional generalization test on a Mixture-of-Experts model (DeepSeekVL2), and full breakdown of POPE across 9 settings x 2 models in the appendix.

Good motivating analysis (Section 2.3, Figure 2) that empirically demonstrates why raw logit-lens projection of vision tokens is uninformative without vocabulary constraint, and grounds the method design in observed decoding dynamics (hallucinations often occur when top-1 diverges from visually plausible top-5 alternatives).

Ablation study examining vocabulary constraint necessity, layer selection strategy, and threshold sensitivity, along with a clear algorithmic description (Algorithm 1) and extensive appendix case studies with concrete logit/probability values, aiding reproducibility and interpretability.
Honest discussion of limitations regarding overfitting to visually salient cues and inability to correct pretraining-derived factual errors.
weaknesses: Performance improvements over the strongest baseline (SID) are frequently marginal or mixed rather than clearly dominant: e.g., CHAIR_S is tied with SID on LLaVA-1.5 (50.6 vs 50.6), AMBER Hal is worse than SID on LLaVA (33.0 vs 32.8), and several POPE precision/F1 entries for Qwen2.5-VL are close to or below SID/DoLa. This tempers the strength of the 'competitive or superior' claim.

The method involves per-model, per-task hyperparameter tuning (layer pool selection 'last' vs 'all', and threshold alpha chosen per task from a log-scale grid), which is not clearly matched by equivalent tuning effort for baselines (stated to use 'default hyperparameters from original implementations'), raising a possible fairness/apples-to-apples concern in the comparison.

Memory/precompute cost of caching full-vocabulary projections for all vision tokens across the candidate layer set J (especially the 'all even layers' setting for Qwen2.5-VL with potentially thousands of dynamic-resolution vision tokens and full vocabulary ~150k) is not discussed or benchmarked; the reported 'per-token' latency may not capture this upfront cost, which could be substantial in memory and non-trivial in time, especially for high-resolution inputs.

The theoretical justification for selecting the vision token minimizing JSD to the current (possibly already hallucinating) output distribution is somewhat heuristic; the paper does not analyze cases where this selection criterion could reinforce rather than correct existing biases in the base output distribution, beyond a brief limitations mention.

The method is a synthesis of existing techniques (DoLa's layer-selection-via-JSD idea, logit-lens, and adaptive plausibility constraint from contrastive decoding) applied to vision tokens rather than intermediate language layers; while the combination and application are useful, the core technical novelty is somewhat incremental.

No comparison against several more recent intra-alignment baselines mentioned in the related work (e.g., HALC, OPERA, dynamic correction decoding), limiting the completeness of the empirical comparison against the current state of the art.

Results rely solely on automatic hallucination metrics (CHAIR/POPE/AMBER) with a single fixed sampling seed and no variance/robustness analysis across sampling seeds or repeated runs, and no human evaluation of overall generation quality/fluency to check whether vocabulary constraining might reduce linguistic diversity or naturalness.

strengths: The motivation analysis (Sec 2) is unusually rigorous for this literature: it uses well-defined at-least-one recall@k metrics with Wilson confidence intervals, paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction, and clearly documented sample sizes (n=190 hallucinated steps, 173,173 vision token projections), giving credible evidence for the core claim that vision tokens encode latent, recoverable object semantics.

The proposed decoding method (ReVisiT) is training-free, requires no architecture change or extra forward passes, and empirically matches vanilla greedy decoding's inference latency (within ~2%) while competing decoding baselines (VCD, M3ID, SID, CODE) incur up to 2x overhead — a clear and well-substantiated efficiency advantage.

Broad empirical validation: results are reported across five benchmarks (HallusionBench, CHAIR, POPE, MMMU, VQAv2) spanning both generative and discriminative tasks, and scalability is demonstrated across seven model checkpoints spanning three architecture families (LLaVA, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL) and sizes from 7B to 32B.

Ablations are reasonably comprehensive, isolating the contribution of vocabulary-subset constraining, the vision-token selection criterion (min/max/random JSD), layer scope, and threshold sensitivity, with a degenerate failure case (full-vocabulary projection) shown quantitatively and qualitatively to justify design choices.
Reproducibility details are strong: full algorithm pseudocode, hyperparameter settings per model, and extensive appendix tables/case studies with exact logit values supporting the qualitative claims.
weaknesses: Quantitative gains are frequently marginal and inconsistent: e.g., in Table 3 CHAIR, ReVisiT is only second-best on CHAIRS for LLaVA (50.6 tied with SID's rank, worse than CODE's 45.2), and on LLaVA-1.5-13B in Table 9, CHAIRS actually worsens (48.0 → 52.6) despite F1 improving slightly, undercutting the 'consistently enhances visual grounding' claim.

Full baseline comparison (against DoLA, VCD, M3ID, CODE, SID) is only conducted for two models (LLaVA-1.5-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B); the headline scalability claim across 7 models/3 architectures (Fig. 1, Table 9) is supported only by comparison to greedy decoding, not to competing decoding baselines, weakening the 'scalability and model-agnostic effectiveness' claim relative to state-of-the-art alternatives.

The core mechanism—constrained vocabulary subset selection via adaptive plausibility constraint (borrowed directly from Li et al. 2023a's contrastive decoding) combined with per-step divergence-based reference token selection—is a reasonable but incremental combination of existing ingredients (logit-lens-style projection, contrastive/plausibility-constrained decoding) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Some reported improvements on general VQA/MMMU tasks are very small (e.g., VQAv2 Qwen2.5-VL 65.80→67.60 vs. SID's 67.13; MMMU differences of ~1 point), making it unclear whether gains are statistically meaningful given no variance/significance reporting for the main results tables (unlike the rigor shown in the motivation section).

The method's dependence on hand-tuned, task-specific and model-specific hyperparameters (layer-selection scheme 'last' vs 'all', and α chosen per task from a log-scale grid) raises reproducibility/generalization concerns for genuinely new tasks or models without such tuning, somewhat undermining the 'simple, training-free' framing.

Qualitative failure cases (Appendix C.2) show that without the vocabulary constraint the method degenerates into repetitive garbage tokens, indicating the method's success is highly dependent on a fairly fragile constrained-decoding heuristic rather than a robust use of vision-token semantics per se.

strengths: Thorough motivational analysis (Sec. 2) with carefully designed quantitative probes (at-least-one recall@k, GT/Hal max-probability comparisons with w/ vs w/o image ablation, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, vision-token logit-lens projections with confidence intervals) that build a coherent narrative for why vision tokens retain visually grounded semantics even when hallucinations occur.

The proposed ReVisiT method is simple, training-free, architecture-agnostic, and empirically very cheap (near-zero latency overhead vs up to 2x for competing contrastive-decoding baselines), which is a meaningful practical advantage over VCD/M3ID/SID/CODE.

Reasonably broad evaluation across five benchmarks (HallusionBench, CHAIR, POPE, MMMU, VQAv2) spanning both discriminative and generative/hallucination-focused and general VQA settings, with two different LVLM backbones (LLaVA-1.5-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B).

Detailed ablations isolating the contribution of vocabulary-subset constraint, token-selection criterion (min/max/random-JSD), layer scope, and threshold α, including a striking failure-mode case study (degenerate repeated tokens) when the vocabulary constraint is removed, supporting the core design choice.
Strong reproducibility support: full algorithm pseudocode, detailed hyperparameter settings, dataset/metric formulas, and extensive per-benchmark tables in the appendix.
weaknesses: Reported gains are frequently marginal and inconsistent: ReVisiT is not actually best on several key metrics (e.g., SID outperforms ReVisiT on CHAIR F1/CHAIR_I for LLaVA-1.5-7B in Table 3, and on POPE accuracy/F1 for Qwen2.5-VL-7B in Table 4; MMMU improvement for Qwen2.5-VL-7B is only 51.11→51.18, essentially noise). The paper's framing ("competitive or superior") somewhat overstates a fairly mixed empirical picture.

The headline "scalability across six model sizes/three architectures" claim (Fig. 1, Table 9) is validated only on the CHAIR benchmark; the full five-benchmark suite is evaluated on just two 7B models, so the generality claim is broader than the evidence supports.

The method requires per-task (and per-model) hand-tuning of the APC threshold α and the choice of candidate decoder layers ("last" vs "all"), which partially undercuts the "simple, training-free" positioning — these are nontrivial design/hyperparameter choices tuned per benchmark rather than a single fixed robust configuration, raising concerns about overfitting to specific benchmarks and practical applicability when ground truth for tuning is unavailable.

The statistical evidence for the central hallucination-mitigation motivation is actually weaker than advertised at the specific decision points that matter most: Table 7 shows the GT-favoring shift is significant over all tokens, but not significant specifically at hallucinated steps (the cases the paper cares about), which is a tension not fully reconciled in the main text.

Some baselines (e.g., CODE) collapse dramatically under certain settings (e.g., F1=48.50 on Qwen2.5-VL CHAIR), suggesting either baseline/hyperparameter mismatch for newer architectures or unfair comparison conditions, which weakens confidence in the comparative claims.

The core refinement mechanism (element-wise multiplication of constrained output distribution with a single selected vision-token's constrained projection, followed by renormalization) is motivated mostly empirically; limited theoretical grounding is given for why this combination rule is principled versus alternative fusion strategies.

No comparison to other recent/strong hallucination mitigation approaches mentioned in related work (e.g., OPERA, HALC, Woodpecker, attention-based methods), despite the paper's claim of comprehensive benchmarking against SOTA decoding strategies.

strengths: The paper grounds its method in a careful empirical analysis (Sec. 2) that provides quantitative evidence (recall@k statistics with confidence intervals, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests) for the two key claims motivating ReVisiT: that ground-truth objects remain in the output distribution even during hallucination, and that vision-token projections reveal interpretable semantics only under vocabulary-constrained projection. This analysis is unusually rigorous for a motivation section and gives real support to the method design rather than being purely intuitive.

ReVisiT is simple, training-free, architecture-agnostic, and achieves near-zero computational overhead (as little as +0.6% latency), in sharp contrast to competing contrastive-decoding baselines (VCD, M3ID, SID, CODE) that roughly double inference cost — this efficiency-performance tradeoff is a genuine practical advantage clearly substantiated with timing measurements (Fig. 6, Table 12).

Broad empirical validation: five benchmarks (HallusionBench, CHAIR, POPE, MMMU, VQAv2) spanning both hallucination-focused and general VQA/discriminative tasks, and scalability results across seven models/three architectures (Fig. 1, Table 9), which supports claims of generality.

Solid ablation study isolating the contributions of the vocabulary constraint, vision-token selection criterion (min- vs max- vs random-JSD), and layer scope, with a degenerate failure case (full-vocabulary projection) that convincingly demonstrates the necessity of the proposed constrained-divergence design.

Reasonably reproducible: detailed algorithm pseudocode, hyperparameter descriptions, and extensive appendix documentation of evaluation protocols, metric formulas, and qualitative case studies with full numeric breakdowns.
weaknesses: Main experimental comparisons against the six decoding baselines (DoLa, VCD, M3ID, CODE, SID) are conducted on only two backbones (LLaVA-1.5-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B); the broader 7-model/3-architecture scalability claim is only verified on a single benchmark (CHAIR), leaving the generality of gains on other benchmarks (POPE, HallusionBench, MMMU, VQAv2) across model scales unconfirmed.

Gains are inconsistent in places and sometimes marginal: on POPE, ReVisiT is outperformed by SID for Qwen2.5-VL-7B; on MMMU Qwen2.5-VL-7B accuracy improves only marginally (51.11→51.18); on CHAIR with LLaVA-1.5-13B, greedy CHAIRS actually outperforms ReVisiT (48.0 vs 52.6) without discussion of why the trend reverses for this configuration.

The method requires two model/task-specific hyperparameters (candidate decoder-layer pool and threshold α), which are tuned per model and per task; while the paper argues sensitivity is modest, the practice of selecting task-specific α (e.g., different settings for generative vs. discriminative tasks) raises some concern about implicit tuning to each benchmark rather than a single robust default.

No variance/repeated-run statistics are reported for the main benchmark tables (only inference latency includes standard deviations), making it hard to assess whether the reported improvements—some of which are within a point or two—are statistically meaningful.

Baseline comparisons, while reasonably comprehensive, are somewhat dated relative to the 2025 decoding-hallucination literature (SID is the only 2025 baseline used), and some very recent alternative logit-lens/attention-based approaches discussed in the related work section (e.g., Jiang et al. 2025a/b) are not empirically compared against.
